{{Distinguish|Jingu-kyo}}{{Short description|Japanese new religious movement which emerged from Shinto}}
[[File:Sayo Kitamura.JPG|thumb|Sayo Kitamura, c. 1945–1950]]
[[File:Muga no Mai.JPG|thumb|The movement's ''muga no mai'' dance, September 1948]]
'''Tenshō Kōtai Jingūkyō''' ({{ill|Japanese language|ja|日本語|lt=Japanese|lt_ja=日本語}} {{lang|ja|天照皇大神宮教}}, ''Tenshō Kōtai Jingūkyō'') is a Japanese {{ill|New religious movement|ja|新宗教|lt=new religious movement|lt_ja=新宗教}} which emerged from {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道|lt=Shinto|lt_ja=神道}}, organised as a {{ill|Religious corporation|ja|宗教法人|lt=religious corporation|lt_ja=宗教法人}} since January 1947. The {{ill|Agency for Cultural Affairs|ja|文化庁|lt=Agency for Cultural Affairs|lt_ja=文化庁}}' ''Shūkyō Nenkan'' (religion yearbook) classes it as "other religions" (''shokyō''). It was founded by {{ill|Sayo Kitamura|ja|北村サヨ|lt=Sayo Kitamura|lt_ja=北村サヨ}} ({{lang|ja|北村 サヨ}}) (1900–1967), with activities beginning in 1945.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/ijcc/wp/glossary/def_T.html|title=Glossary of Shinto Names and Terms: T|website=www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp|language=ja|access-date=2018-10-16}}</ref> Kitamura claimed possession by {{ill|Amaterasu|ja|天照大神|lt=Amaterasu|lt_ja=天照大神}} under the title Tenshō-Kōtaijin.

Its headquarters are at 10123 Hano, {{ill|Tabuse, Yamaguchi|ja|田布施町|lt=Tabuse|lt_ja=田布施町}} ({{lang|ja|田布施町}}, ''Tabuse-chō''), {{ill|Kumage District, Yamaguchi|ja|熊毛郡 (山口県)|lt=Kumage District|lt_ja=熊毛郡}}, {{ill|Yamaguchi Prefecture|ja|山口県|lt=Yamaguchi Prefecture|lt_ja=山口県}}, {{ill|Japan|ja|日本|lt=Japan|lt_ja=日本}}. It also has a Yamaguchi dōjō at 188 Hirai, {{ill|Yamaguchi, Yamaguchi|ja|山口市|lt=Yamaguchi|lt_ja=山口市}}, and a Tokyo dōjō at 4-3-18 {{ill|Kudankita|ja|九段北|lt=Kudankita|lt_ja=九段北}}, {{ill|Chiyoda, Tokyo|ja|千代田区|lt=Chiyoda|lt_ja=千代田区}}.

Followers practise a dance called ''muga no mai'' ({{lang|ja|無我の舞}}, "dance of the non-self" or "dance of non-ego"), which is why the religion is called the "dancing religion" ({{lang|ja|踊る宗教}}, ''odoru shūkyō'').

== Overview ==
The founder, {{ill|Sayo Kitamura|ja|北村サヨ|lt=Sayo Kitamura|lt_ja=北村サヨ}} (called Ōgami-sama, "Great God"; 1 January 1900 – 28 December 1967), was a farm wife of Tabuse, born at Ōsato, Hizumi village, {{ill|Kuga District, Yamaguchi|ja|玖珂郡|lt=Kuga District|lt_ja=玖珂郡}} (now Hizumi, {{ill|Yanai, Yamaguchi|ja|柳井市|lt=Yanai|lt_ja=柳井市}}). The second leader was her granddaughter Kitamura Kiyokazu (called Himegami-sama; 27 April 1950 – 7 June 2006),<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kitamura Kiyokazu-san shikyo / Tenshō Kōtai Jingūkyō kyōshu |url=https://www.shikoku-np.co.jp/national/okuyami/article.aspx?id=20060607000501 |website=Shikoku Shimbun |access-date=2024-09-17 |date=2006-06-07}}</ref> daughter of Sayo's eldest son Kitamura Yoshito (called Wakagami-sama; representative officer of the religious corporation).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kitamura Yoshito-shi shikyo / Tenshō Kōtai Jingūkyō daihyō yakuin |url=http://www.shikoku-np.co.jp/national/okuyami/article.aspx?id=20070715000002 |website=Shikoku Shimbun |access-date=2024-09-17 |date=2007-07-15}}</ref> The third leader is Kiyokazu's daughter Kitamura Meiwa (called Meiwa-sama; born 9 January 1990), leader since 2 January 2009. The representative officers have been Kitamura Yoshito (1947–2007) and, since 2009, Kitamura Tetsumasa.

In 1946, which the movement calls "the first year of the era of the Kingdom of God", it began to use its own {{ill|Shinengō|ja|私年号|lt=private era name|lt_ja=私年号}}, "Kigen".

The name of the movement was given by the god that entered the founder's belly, in order to show people who had received the nationalist historical education of the years before the end of the Second World War<ref>Education that made the emperor a living god (''arahitogami'') and Amaterasu the ancestor of the imperial house and so the supreme deity.</ref> that its teaching was that of the highest god of the universe. In substance the movement has no connection at all with {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道|lt=Shinto|lt_ja=神道}} (the {{ill|Kōtai Jingū|ja|皇大神宮|lt=Kōtai Jingū|lt_ja=皇大神宮}} or {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|ja|伊勢神宮|lt=Ise Grand Shrine|lt_ja=伊勢神宮}}), or with other established or new religions, and in particular none with the gods of Japanese mythology as told in the ''Nihon Shoki'' and the ''Kojiki''.

That is, the god of Tenshō Kōtai Jingūkyō is held to be the absolute god of the universe, the same as the {{ill|Original Buddha|ja|本仏|lt=original Buddha|lt_ja=本仏}} of {{ill|Buddhism|ja|仏教|lt=Buddhism|lt_ja=仏教}} or the God in heaven of {{ill|Christianity|ja|キリスト教|lt=Christianity|lt_ja=キリスト教}}. The movement's scripture, the ''Seisho'' (生書), has the god tell Sayo not to think of Tenshō Kōtai Jingū as the guardian god of the little islands of Japan: there is only one god ruling the universe, and the God of Christ and the original Buddha of Buddhism are all one.<ref>''Seisho'', vol. 1, 11th ed., pp. 76–77.</ref>

== The Kingdom of God ==
Tenshō Kōtai Jingūkyō holds that "world peace begins with peace in one's own heart", and teaches that the first thing is to become a person with a pure and upright heart. From the peace of the individual heart it aims to widen out to peace in the family, at school, at work and in the community.

The aim of the god that entered the founder's belly is to build the Kingdom of God on earth. With the forming of a world of comrades who live each day in ''shinkō'' (神行, "divine practice") centred on the founder's teaching, it says, "the Kingdom of God has come about"; the spreading of this world is the building of the Kingdom of God on earth.

== Founder ==
After six years of {{ill|Elementary school|ja|小学校|lt=elementary school|lt_ja=小学校}}, {{ill|Sayo Kitamura|ja|北村サヨ|lt=Sayo Kitamura|lt_ja=北村サヨ}} married into a farming family. After a fire at her house, thought to be arson, she began ''ushi no toki mairi'' (midnight shrine visits) and water austerities. On 4 May 1944 (Shōwa 19), something began to speak from her belly, and she began to preach to people.<ref>''Seisho'', vol. 1, 11th ed., p. 48.</ref> On the 10th she is said to have chanted "Myō Myōhō Renketsu-kyō" (名妙法連結経; '''not''' the Buddhist "{{ill|Namu Myōhō Renge Kyō|ja|南無妙法蓮華経|lt=Namu Myōhō Renge Kyō|lt_ja=南無妙法蓮華経}}").

According to the first volume of the ''Seisho'', Sayo received from the god "spectacles that show the whole world at a glance", and could see everything in the universe, and people's past conduct back to their previous lives.<ref>''Seisho'', vol. 1, 11th ed., p. 151.</ref>

She later toured repeatedly, in Japan and abroad, spreading her teaching; these journeys are recorded in the first four volumes of the ''Seisho''. For the twenty-four years from May 1944 until her death she is said to have preached every day.

== Membership ==
According to the Agency for Cultural Affairs' ''Shūkyō Nenkan'' (2022 edition, pp. 86–87), the movement reported 490,807 members at the end of 2021, more than {{ill|Seicho-no-Ie|ja|生長の家|lt=Seichō-no-Ie|lt_ja=生長の家}} (348,119), {{ill|En'ōkyō|ja|円応教|lt=En'ōkyō|lt_ja=円応教}} (439,767) or {{ill|Konkokyo|ja|金光教|lt=Konkōkyō|lt_ja=金光教}} (374,643). Sayo herself toured {{ill|Hawaii|ja|ハワイ州|lt=Hawaii|lt_ja=ハワイ州}} in the {{ill|United States|ja|アメリカ合衆国|lt=United States|lt_ja=アメリカ合衆国}}, where many {{ill|Immigration|ja|移民|lt=emigrants|lt_ja=移民}} from Yamaguchi Prefecture had settled, and there are a certain number of followers there, mainly {{ill|Nikkei|ja|日系人|lt=Japanese Americans|lt_ja=日系人}};<ref>Nishiyama Shigeru and Fujii Takeshi (trans. N. Havens), "The Propagation and Spread of Tenshō Kōtai Jingūkyō within Japanese-American Society on Hawaii Island", ''Bulletin of the Institute for Japanese Culture and Classics'' 64, {{ill|Kokugakuin University|ja|國學院大學|lt=Kokugakuin University|lt_ja=國學院大學}}, 1989, pp. 390–430.</ref> a dōjō was opened there in 1976.<ref>Tenshō Kōtai Jingūkyō, ''Tenshō Kōtai Jingūkyō Hawai Dōjō Shunkō Kinen'' (1976).</ref>

== Other ==
One feature of the movement is that it does not cooperate with any other religious body. Asked by a newspaper reporter what relations it had with other religions, the founder answered that it had none and would join hands with none: in the last days religions had become human religions or dead religions, so the God of heaven had descended to teach the true religion directly.<ref>''Seisho'', vol. 4, 1st ed., p. 221.</ref>
